exampleAnswers.title: Calculating the Cross Product of Two Vectors Whose Angle Is a Special Angle

question.text: The vector $\mathbf{a}$ has magnitude $3$, the vector $\mathbf{b}$ has magnitude $6$, the angle between $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ is $30^\circ$ and $\mathbf{n}$ is the unit vector that points in the direction of $\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}.$ Find $\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$ in terms of $\mathbf{n}.$
question.explanation:
We use the formula for the cross product and obtain

\[ \eqalign{ \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} & = |\mathbf{a}| \cdot |\mathbf{b}| \cdot \sin{\theta} \cdot \mathbf{n} \\[3pt] &= 3 \cdot 6 \cdot \sin{30^\circ} \cdot \mathbf{n} \\[3pt] &= 18 \cdot 0.5 \cdot \mathbf{n} \\[3pt] &= 9\mathbf{n}. } \]

example.title: Calculating the Cross Product of Two Vectors Whose Angle Is a Special Angle

question.text: The vector $\mathbf{a}$ has magnitude $7$, the vector $\mathbf{b}$ has magnitude $2$, the angle between $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ is $135^\circ$ and $\mathbf{n}$ is the unit vector that points in the direction of $\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}.$ Find $\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$ in terms of $\mathbf{n}.$
question.explanation:
We use the formula for the cross product and obtain

\[ \eqalign{ \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} & = |\mathbf{a}| \cdot |\mathbf{b}| \cdot \sin{\theta} \cdot \mathbf{n} \\[3pt] &= 7 \cdot 2 \cdot \sin{135^\circ} \cdot \mathbf{n} \\[3pt] &= 14 \cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \cdot \mathbf{n} \\[3pt] &= 7\sqrt{2}\mathbf{n}. } \]

exampleAnswers.title: Calculating the Cross Product of Two Vectors Whose Angle Is a Non-Special Angle

question.text: The vector $\mathbf{u}$ has magnitude $5$, the vector $\mathbf{v}$ has magnitude $4,$ the angle between $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ is $160^\circ$ and $\mathbf{n}$ is the unit vector that points in the direction of $\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}.$ Find $\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}$ in terms of $\mathbf{n}.$ Round your final answer to one decimal place where appropriate.
question.explanation:
We use the formula for the cross product and obtain

\[ \eqalign{ \mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v} &= |\mathbf{u}| \cdot |\mathbf{v}| \cdot \sin{\theta} \cdot \mathbf{n} \\[3pt] &= 5 \cdot 4 \cdot \sin{160^\circ} \cdot \mathbf{n} \\[3pt] & = 20 \cdot (0.342\,02 \ldots) \cdot \mathbf{n} \\[3pt] & = (6.840\,40 \ldots) \cdot \mathbf{n} \\[3pt] & \approx 6.8 \mathbf{n}. } \]

example.title: Calculating the Cross Product of Two Vectors Whose Angle Is a Non-Special Angle

question.text: The vector $\mathbf{u}$ has magnitude $13,$ the vector $\mathbf{v}$ has magnitude $2,$ the angle between $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ is $96^\circ$ and $\mathbf{n}$ is the unit vector that points in the direction of $\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}.$ Find $\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}$ in terms of $\mathbf{n}.$ Round your final answer to two decimal places where appropriate.
question.explanation:
We use the formula for the cross product and obtain

\[ \eqalign{ \mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v} &= |\mathbf{u}| \cdot |\mathbf{v}| \cdot \sin{\theta} \cdot \mathbf{n} \\[3pt] &= 13 \cdot 2 \cdot \sin{96^\circ} \cdot \mathbf{n} \\[3pt] & = 26 \cdot (0.994\,52 \ldots) \cdot \mathbf{n} \\[3pt] & = (25.857\,56 \ldots) \cdot \mathbf{n} \\[3pt] & \approx 25.86 \mathbf{n}. } \]

exampleAnswers.title: Calculating the Cross Product of Two Parallel Vectors

question.text: The vector $\mathbf{u}$ has magnitude $1,$ the vector $\mathbf{v}$ has magnitude $5,$ and $\mathbf{u} \parallel \mathbf{v}.$ Find $\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}.$
question.explanation:
Suppose $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ are nonzero vectors. Then, $\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ if and only if $\mathbf{u} \parallel \mathbf{v}.$

Therefore, $\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}.$

example.title: Calculating the Cross Product of Two Parallel Vectors

question.text: The vector $\mathbf{c}$ has magnitude $3,$ the vector $\mathbf{d}$ has magnitude $4,$ and $\mathbf{c} \parallel \mathbf{d}.$ Find $\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{d}.$
question.explanation:
Suppose $\mathbf c$ and $\mathbf d$ are nonzero vectors. Then, $\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{0}$ if and only if $\mathbf{c} \parallel \mathbf{d}.$

Therefore, $\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{0}.$
